name: Council of Ephesus
summary: The council at which Cyril of Alexandria had Nestorius of Constantinople deposed and Mary affirmed as Theotokos ('God-bearer'), held amid rival assemblies, imperial arrests, and bribery of the court.

end.date: Dissolved by the emperor c. September–October 431

background.text: Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople from 428, objected to calling Mary Theotokos ('God-bearer') and preferred Christotokos ('Christ-bearer'); Cyril of Alexandria accused him of dividing Christ into two persons.
A Roman synod under Pope Celestine I condemned Nestorius in August 430 and asked Cyril to enforce it; Cyril added twelve anathemas that Nestorius and the bishops of Antioch rejected.
Emperor Theodosius II summoned a council to Ephesus for Pentecost 431.

happened.text: On 22 June 431 Cyril opened the council with about 150 bishops, over the protest of the imperial commissioner Candidian and 68 bishops, before John of Antioch and the Syrian bishops arrived. That same day it deposed Nestorius, who refused to attend.
John of Antioch arrived on 26 June and held a rival council of about 43 bishops with Candidian's support, which deposed Cyril and Memnon, bishop of Ephesus.
Pope Celestine's legates arrived in July and endorsed Cyril's council.
A letter from Capreolus of Carthage was read explaining that the African bishops could not come; Theodosius's invitation to Augustine had arrived after Augustine's death in August 430.
Cyril's council also condemned Pelagian teaching and forbade composing any creed other than that of Nicaea (canon 7).

In August Theodosius accepted both sides' depositions and had Cyril, Memnon, and Nestorius held under guard. Cyril's agents spent heavily on gifts to court officials; a list of these 'blessings' survives. Cyril escaped back to Alexandria, Nestorius was sent to his monastery near Antioch, and the emperor dissolved the council.

participants.name: Theodosius II
participants.role: Eastern Roman emperor; summoned the council

participants.name: Celestine I
participants.role: Bishop of Rome; sent legates who backed Cyril

participants.name: Augustine of Hippo
participants.role: Invited by Theodosius II, but died before the invitation arrived

outcomes.text: In the Formula of Reunion (433) Cyril and John of Antioch were reconciled; John accepted Nestorius's deposition and Cyril accepted a statement of Christ's two natures.
Calling Mary Theotokos became standard in Catholic and Orthodox teaching and devotion.
The Church of the East in Persia never accepted the council and is still sometimes, inaccurately, called 'Nestorian'.
The quarrel over how to read Cyril led directly to the Council of Ephesus of 449 and to Chalcedon (451).

condemnations.authority: Council of bishops, backed by the papal legates
condemnations.reason: Nestorius deposed and excommunicated for teaching that divided Christ and for rejecting the title Theotokos
condemnations.status: Confirmed by Theodosius II and by Chalcedon (451); the Church of the East honors Nestorius as a teacher

condemnations.reason: Cyril of Alexandria and Memnon of Ephesus deposed for heresy and for opening the council early
condemnations.status: Not upheld; withdrawn in the reunion of 433

condemnations.reason: John of Antioch and his supporters suspended from communion

persecution_note: No one was killed. The emperor's arrests in 431 hit both sides; the lasting penalties fell on Nestorius and his supporters.

persecution.title: Arrest of Cyril, Memnon, and Nestorius
persecution.summary: The imperial official John, sent by Theodosius II, placed all three bishops under guard after the emperor accepted both councils' depositions. Cyril's party then won the court over, helped by large gifts to officials.

responsible.name: Count John
responsible.role: Imperial official who carried out the arrests

persecution.outcome: Cyril escaped to Alexandria and kept his see; Nestorius was sent to his monastery near Antioch.

persecution.title: Exile of Nestorius and ban on his books
persecution.summary: Theodosius II ordered Nestorius's books burned and his followers to be called 'Simonians', and exiled him first to Petra and then to the Great Oasis in Egypt, where he was caught up in raids by nomads.

responsible.name: Cyril of Alexandria and his supporters
